content.text: When ice melts or water boils, energy is absorbed but the temperature doesn't change. Where does this energy go? It goes into changing the state of the substance—breaking bonds between particles. The energy required for these changes of state is called latent heat.

Specific latent heat is the energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature. There are two types: latent heat of fusion (solid to liquid) and latent heat of vaporisation (liquid to gas). The equation is E = mL.
is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state, without a change in temperature.
"Latent" means "hidden"—the energy is hidden because temperature doesn't change
Energy goes into breaking/forming bonds between particles
Different substances require different amounts of latent heat
Energy to change 1 kg of solid to liquid (or vice versa) at the melting point
Energy to change 1 kg of liquid to gas (or vice versa) at the boiling point
Lv is always much larger than Lf for the same substance because:
More bonds need to be broken going from liquid to gas
Particles must be completely separated in a gas
Specific latent heat has units of
Latent Heat Values for Common Substances
Note: For water, Lv is about 7 times larger than Lf.

Note: Most energy goes into vaporisation, not heating!

                  Energy added (J)

  Flat sections: energy = mL (state change)
  Sloped sections: energy = mcΔθ (temperature change)
Gradient of sloping sections relates to specific heat capacity
Length of flat sections relates to latent heat
Longer flat section = more latent heat

Do not confuse specific heat capacity (E = mc delta T, which changes temperature) with specific latent heat (E = mL, which changes state). During a change of state, use E = mL, not E = mc delta T, because the temperature is not changing.

The latent heat of vaporisation is always much larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance, because completely separating particles (liquid to gas) requires much more energy than simply loosening their arrangement (solid to liquid).

Steam at 100°C causes worse burns than water at 100°C because:
Steam releases latent heat when it condenses on your skin
1 g of steam releases 2260 J when condensing
Then the water releases more heat as it cools
Much more energy is transferred to your skin
Absorbs latent heat while melting (334 kJ/kg)
Then absorbs more heat as cold water warms up
Evaporation of sweat cools the body:
Sweat absorbs latent heat of vaporisation from skin
Energy is removed from the body
Water absorbs huge amounts of latent heat when boiling
Energy is released when steam condenses
Transfer heat from inside to outside
— During state changes, more energy doesn't increase temperature; it changes the state.
"Ice at 0°C and water at 0°C have the same energy"
— Water at 0°C has MORE internal energy (the latent heat used to melt the ice).
— It's stored as potential energy between particles, and released during the reverse change.
"Boiling happens quickly because water heats up fast"
— Boiling is slow because huge amounts of latent heat must be supplied.
"Steam cools you down like water does"
— No! Steam releases latent heat when it condenses on your skin, causing severe burns.

Latent heat = energy for state change without temperature change
Two types: fusion (Lf) for melting/freezing, vaporisation (Lv) for boiling/condensing
Lv >> Lf (more energy needed to vaporise than melt)
For water: Lf = 334,000 J/kg, Lv = 2,260,000 J/kg
Energy goes into breaking/forming bonds between particles
Heating curves show flat sections during state changes
Applications: cooling, refrigeration, steam power, sweating

— Stage 1: steam condenses at 100°C: E₁ = mLv = 0.05 × 2,260,000 = 113,000 J. Stage 2: water cools from 100°C to 40°C: E₂ = mcΔθ = 0.05 × 4200 × 60 = 12,600 J. Total = 113,000 + 12,600 = 125,600 J (calculation)
Ice absorbs latent heat of fusion as it melts (334,000 J/kg), in addition to absorbing energy as the meltwater warms up.

Cold water at 0°C can only absorb energy through a temperature rise (using E = mcΔθ). The extra latent heat absorbed by melting ice removes significantly more energy from the drink, making ice a more effective coolant. (explanation with physics reasoning)

— Lf = E/m = 70,000/0.2 = 350,000 J/kg. This is slightly higher than the accepted value of 334,000 J/kg. Possible reasons: some energy from the heater heated the surroundings rather than melting ice; the container absorbed some heat; not all the measured energy went solely into melting. (comparison)
